newsitem.title: ITALY: Golden share may clash with free market - Monti.
newsitem.headline: Golden share may clash with free market - Monti.

text.p: European Commissioner Mario Monti warned on Thursday that using a "golden share" to maintain state control in a privatised company could clash with the principles of free competition.

Monti said keeping a golden share could serve to prolong situations in which domestic shareholders have privileges over non-domestics, for instance in approving the entrance of other shareholders into a company's capital.
Speaking in an Italian parliamentary hearing, he said: "In privatisations, you cannot discriminate against non-nationals."
"For controlling stakes, you cannot discriminate against investors in the European Union. For non-controlling stakes you cannot even discriminate against countries outside the EU."

When national economic policymakers said they wanted to limit access to companies up for privatisation to nationals, this created "a surplus of vigilance and situations of uncertainty among investors which are already potentially harmful to the free movement of capital."

Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said on Wednesday the government favoured keeping a golden share in state telecommunications holding Stet, which it expects to privatise in the autumn of this year.

However Italy's constitutional court has allowed a proposed referendum seeking to abolish the use of golden shares, which give the Treasury special powers in privatised companies deemed to be of public interest. Ciampi said the referendum would take place and the government would abide by the outcome.

Monti, turning to the single market, said in June in Amsterdam the Commission would present the European council with a plan of action to achieve a more effective single market by January 1, 1999, whose thrust will be about observing EU rules.
The single market was introduced in January 1993 but Monti has said in the past the market is not yet fully implemented and has not developed its full potential.
In addition, Italy "is not in a satisfactory position" as far as respecting European directives was concerned, he said.
"Altogether on directives on a single market, Italy is in 13th place with a deficit of 10.7 percent," he said.
